Walsall's population increased by around 14,800 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 280,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Walsall increased by 5.5%, from around 269,300 in 2011 to around 284,100 in 2021.

The population here increased at a similar rate to the overall population of the West Midlands (6.2%), but by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Walsall was home to around 19.5 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 18.5 in 2011. This area was among the top 25% most densely populated English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Walsall than across the West Midlands

Median age in Walsall

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Walsall decreased by one year, from 39 to 38 years of age.

This area had a lower average (median) age than the West Midlands as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and a lower average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 6,300 (an increase of 13.5%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by just over 1,800 (3.3% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 1.3 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Employment in Walsall

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed increased in Walsall, but fell across the West Midlands.

In Walsall, the percentage who were employed rose from 51.2% in 2011 to 51.7% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 54.4% to 53.3%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in Walsall fell from 6.1% to 3.9%, while the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were retired (economically inactive) decreased from 22.8% to 20.8%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Walsall increased by 0.5 percentage points

Working hours in Walsall

In 2021, 9.0% of Walsall residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (8.9%).

In 2021, around 1 in 11 people (9.0%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 10.5% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 59.4% to 60.7%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week increased from 9.6% to 9.9% across the West Midlands. Across England, the percentage increased from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Walsall increased by 0.1 percentage points

More lone parents

Walsall saw England's joint third-largest percentage-point rise (alongside Bradford) in the proportion of lone-parent households (from 12.0% in 2011 to 14.0% in 2021).

England's largest increases in the percentage of lone-parent households occurred in Thurrock (from 11.2% to 13.5%) followed by Isles of Scilly (from 3.4% to 5.6%).

Because of its small size, comparisons to Isles of Scilly should be made with caution.

The percentage of households including a lone parent in Walsall increased by 2.0 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Walsall saw the West Midlands' second-largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership (from 32.9% in 2011 to 37.5% in 2021).

Across the region, only Dudley saw a greater rise in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership (from 31.2% to 35.9%).

Every local authority area across the West Midlands saw a rise in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership, as the regional percentage grew from 33.7% to 37.1%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Walsall increased by 4.6 percentage points

Change in unpaid care

Walsall saw the West Midlands' joint largest percentage-point rise (alongside Wyre Forest) in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 2.0% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Telford and Wrekin (from 1.8% to 2.3%), Dudley (from 1.8% to 2.3%), Solihull (from 1.5% to 2.0%) and Wolverhampton (from 1.9% to 2.4%) saw the West Midlands' next largest increases in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care.

Every local authority area across the West Midlands saw a rise in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion grew from 1.7% to 2.1%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of those providing between 20 and 49 hours of weekly unpaid care in Walsall increased by 0.6 percentage points

National identity in Walsall

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater in Walsall (3.6 percentage points) than in nearby Lichfield (0.6 percentage points).

In Walsall, the percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity increased from 4.5% in 2011 to 8.1% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage in nearby Lichfield increased from 2.0% to 2.6%.

The percentage of people who identified with a UK and non-UK national identity in Walsall increased from 0.5% to 1.2%, while the percentage of people who identified as "British only" increased from 18.3% to 56.5%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Walsall increased by 3.6 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Of Walsall households, 16.3% rented privately in 2021, up from 11.7% in 2011.

The increase in the percentage of privately-rented homes was greater in Walsall (4.7 percentage points) than across the West Midlands (3.9 percentage points, from 14.0% to 17.9%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.6 percentage points, from 16.8% to 20.5%.

Private renting in Walsall increased by 4.7 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Walsall

In 2021, 18.7% of Walsall residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 15.2% in 2011. The 3.5 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the West Midlands, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 10.8% to 13.3%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 71.4% of people in Walsall identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 78.9% in 2011), while 4.6% identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category (compared with 2.4% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category increased from 2.7% in 2011 to 3.3% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

Read the bulletin Ethnic group, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 18.7% of usual residents in Walsall identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category

Religion in Walsall

In 2021, 30.2% of Walsall residents reported having "No religion", up from 20.0% in 2011. The rise of 10.2 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Walsall. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the West Midlands, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 22.0% to 32.9%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 44.7% of people in Walsall described themselves as Christian (down from 59.0%), while 11.3% described themselves as Muslim (up from 8.2% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 30.2% of usual residents in Walsall reported having "No religion"

Walsall residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 239,700 Walsall residents said they were born in England. This represented 84.4% of the local population. The figure has decreased from around 239,800 in 2011, which at the time represented 89.0% of Walsall's population.

India was the next most represented, with just over 9,600 Walsall residents reporting this country of birth (3.4%). This figure was up from just under 7,500 in 2011, which at the time represented 2.8% of the population of Walsall.

The number of Walsall residents born in Pakistan rose from just under 5,500 in 2011 (2.0% of the local population) to just under 6,900 in 2021 (2.4%).

In 2021, 84.4% of Walsall residents reported their country of birth as England

Disability in Walsall

In 2021, 9.4% of Walsall residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 11.5% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under one in nine people (10.7%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 11.2% in 2011. The proportion of Walsall residents who were not disabled increased from 77.3% to 79.9%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Walsall (2.1 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the West Midlands (1.9 percentage points, from 9.9% to 8.0%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Walsall decreased by 2.1 percentage points

Health in Walsall

In 2021, 41.9% of Walsall residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 39.3% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 35.8% to 35.4%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Walsall residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.7% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 6.1% to 5.4%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Walsall increased by 2.6 percentage points
